collection: NCEE original Primary 6 reference-based BST conceptual practice
note: Seven finer provisional mappings support 28 original conceptual MCQs. Historical Primary 6 source is not proof of current adoption or official NCEE full scope. Four options and one mark are author choices. No hands-on practical completion or academic approval is claimed.

questions.subject: Basic Science and Technology
questions.learningObjective: Distinguish the Sun, planets and moons and interpret elementary gravitational effects.
questions.prompt: A model labels the Sun as a planet and Earth as a star. Which correction is needed?
options: The Sun is a star and Earth is a planet.
Both are moons.
Earth is a star but the Sun is a moon.
Both are comets.
questions.answer: The Sun is a star and Earth is a planet.
questions.explanation: The Sun produces light as a star; Earth is a planet orbiting it.
questions.practiceFormatNote: Four-option conceptual practice with one author-assigned mark; official NCEE option count and full topic blueprint unverified. Does not assess completion of a practical task.

questions.subject: Basic Science and Technology
questions.learningObjective: Distinguish the Sun, planets and moons and interpret elementary gravitational effects.
questions.prompt: Which relationship should a simple model of Earth and its Moon show?
options: Earth travels around the Moon instead of the Sun.
The Moon is fixed permanently above Nigeria.
The Sun travels around the Moon once each night.
The Moon travels around Earth while Earth travels around the Sun.
questions.answer: The Moon travels around Earth while Earth travels around the Sun.
questions.explanation: Earth has a natural satellite, the Moon; Earth and its Moon also travel around the Sun.
questions.practiceFormatNote: Four-option conceptual practice with one author-assigned mark; official NCEE option count and full topic blueprint unverified. Does not assess completion of a practical task.

questions.subject: Basic Science and Technology
questions.learningObjective: Distinguish the Sun, planets and moons and interpret elementary gravitational effects.
questions.prompt: A soft ball released from a pupil’s hand falls towards the ground. Which force mainly causes the fall?
options: Light pushing the ball down
Sound pulling the ball sideways
Earth’s gravitational pull
Magnetic attraction to every ball

questions.explanation: Gravity attracts the ball towards Earth; the ball need not be magnetic.

questions.subject: Basic Science and Technology
questions.learningObjective: Distinguish the Sun, planets and moons and interpret elementary gravitational effects.
questions.prompt: A learner says the Moon lights the night by making its own sunlight. Which explanation is correct?
options: Earth switches the Moon on every evening.
We see sunlight reflected from the Moon.
The Moon is a second Sun.
The Moon burns classroom fuel.
questions.answer: We see sunlight reflected from the Moon.
questions.explanation: The Moon is visible mainly because it reflects light from the Sun, not because it is a star.

questions.subject: Basic Science and Technology
questions.learningObjective: Relate Earth rotation and revolution to observations and distinguish eclipse alignments.
questions.prompt: A torch shines steadily on a globe. A marked place moves from the lit side to the dark side as the globe turns. What does this represent?
options: A place moving from day into night as Earth rotates.
Earth leaving the solar system.
The Moon making its own light.
A year ending every time a torch is switched off.
questions.answer: A place moving from day into night as Earth rotates.
questions.explanation: Earth’s rotation carries places into and out of sunlight.

questions.subject: Basic Science and Technology
questions.learningObjective: Relate Earth rotation and revolution to observations and distinguish eclipse alignments.
questions.prompt: Which action in a classroom model represents Earth’s revolution?
options: Spinning the globe without moving its centre.
Turning off the model Sun.
Moving only a model Moon around the globe.
Moving the globe around a model Sun.
questions.answer: Moving the globe around a model Sun.
questions.explanation: Revolution is Earth’s orbital motion around the Sun; spinning represents rotation.

Earth’s North Pole
The Moon
Mars

questions.prompt: A pupil records the weather only on rainy days. Why is this a weak record of the whole month?

A month contains only rainy days.
A record needs no observations.
It leaves out the conditions on other days.
questions.answer: It leaves out the conditions on other days.
questions.explanation: Selecting only rainy days gives an incomplete picture of the month.

questions.subject: Basic Science and Technology
questions.learningObjective: Interpret simple weather records and distinguish short-term observations from long-term climate evidence.
questions.prompt: Three afternoons are unusually hot. What is the most careful conclusion?
options: No other place can have rain that week.
The next year must be hot every day.
Hot weather was observed on those afternoons.
The area’s long-term climate is proved to have changed.
questions.answer: Hot weather was observed on those afternoons.
questions.explanation: A few observations describe short-term weather; climate trends require much longer records.

questions.subject: Basic Science and Technology
questions.learningObjective: Interpret simple weather records and distinguish short-term observations from long-term climate evidence.
questions.prompt: Two pupils compare rainfall records from different years. Which practice makes the comparison more dependable?
options: Replace missing measurements with guesses marked as exact.
Use consistently collected records for the same place and comparable periods.
Compare a single hour with an entire year without adjustment.
Remove all days with no rain from both records.
questions.answer: Use consistently collected records for the same place and comparable periods.
questions.explanation: Consistent methods, location and periods make comparisons meaningful.

questions.subject: Basic Science and Technology
questions.learningObjective: Explain changes caused by forces and weigh useful and unwanted friction effects.
questions.prompt: Why do bicycle brakes press pads against a moving wheel rim?
options: The pads turn the wheel into a magnet.
Friction always makes wheels speed up.
Friction helps slow the wheel.
The pads make the wheel weightless.
questions.answer: Friction helps slow the wheel.
questions.explanation: Contact friction opposes the relative motion and helps braking.

questions.subject: Basic Science and Technology
questions.learningObjective: Explain changes caused by forces and weigh useful and unwanted friction effects.
questions.prompt: A machine’s moving parts become worn where they rub. Why might suitable lubrication help?
options: It always increases the rubbing force.
It reduces unwanted friction between the parts.
It removes the need for every moving part.
It makes the machine produce energy from nothing.
questions.answer: It reduces unwanted friction between the parts.
questions.explanation: Lubrication can reduce friction and wear; friction has both useful and unwanted effects.

questions.prompt: A farm uses a computer to compare records of crops grown in different fields. What is the computer helping with?

Making rainfall occur on command.

questions.learningObjective: Relate information technology uses and careers to stated community needs and recognise human responsibility.
questions.prompt: A learner says a computer’s answer must be correct even when the information entered is wrong. Which reply is best?
options: Only the screen colour determines correctness.
Incorrect input can lead to an incorrect result, so people must check the information.
Computers turn every mistake into a fact.
Checking data is never useful.
questions.answer: Incorrect input can lead to an incorrect result, so people must check the information.
questions.explanation: Computers process supplied data; human checking and reliable input remain important.
